books.section: Topic 7.6 World War I: Home Front
United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: J. Allen St. John, "The Hun—his Mark. Blot it Out with Liberty Bonds" poster, ca. 1917

stimulus.text: The poster shows a large red handprint, like a bloody hand pressed to the page. Below it, large lettering reads: "The Hun—his Mark / Blot it Out / with / LIBERTY BONDS." The poster was drawn by J. Allen St. John in about 1917.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by J. Allen St. John, ca. 1917, U.S. Food Administration (NARA 512466), public domain.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, J. Allen St. John poster, ca. 1917, public domain
stem: The poster's image of a bloody handprint was most likely meant to

options.text: show that American soldiers had already defeated Germany
options.misconception: The poster shows a bloody handprint, not a victory; the war was still being fought.

options.text: warn Americans that German armies were landing on American shores
options.misconception: Background from the books: no German army landed in the United States. The handprint stands for German violence abroad, not an invasion.

options.text: prove that the United States had stayed neutral in the war
options.misconception: The poster urges Americans to fund the war, which is the opposite of staying neutral.

options.text: make the German enemy seem violent so Americans would give money

rationales.A: A bloody handprint does not show a victory. It shows violence, and the poster was made while the war was still being fought.
rationales.B: Background from the books: no German army landed in the United States. The handprint stands for German violence abroad, not an invasion.
rationales.C: A poster urging Americans to buy war bonds is a poster for joining the war effort, not for staying neutral.
rationales.D: The bloody handprint paints the German as a violent killer. That fear is the reason the poster gives for buying bonds.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the image. A bloody handprint is a mark of violence, not of victory.
2. Read the words under it. The poster ties that mark to buying Liberty Bonds.
3. Put the two together. The fear the image creates is the push to give money.
Remember: in a persuasion poster, ask what feeling the image is meant to create and what action it points to.
